What ought they to expect, who have wasted them in luxury, if they are condemned who through slothfulness have kept them? "As I was musing, the fire burned." And as he was in this state of wavering suspense, between speaking and holding his peace, between those who are prepared to cavil and those who are anxious to be instructed,...in this state of suspense, he prays for a better place, a place different from this his present stewardship, in which man is in such difficulty and in such danger, and sighing after a certain "end," when he was not to be subject to these things, when the Lord is to say to the faithful dispenser, "Enter thou into the joy of your Lord," [Matthew 25:27] he says, "Then spoke I with my tongue." In this fluctuation, in the midst of these dangers and these difficulties, because, that in consequence of the abundance of offenses "the love of many is waxing cold," [Matthew 24:12] although the law of the Lord inspires delight, in this fluctuation then, (I say), "then spoke I with my tongue." To whom? Not to the hearer whom I would fain instruct; but to Him who hears and takes heed also, by whom I would fain be instructed myself. "I spoke with my tongue" to Him, from whom I inwardly hear whatever I hear that is good or true.— What did You say?
Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 10

A soul entangled in many sins can prepare for itself a certain ointment once it begins to reflect on its behavior, and collects its many and manifold sins, hems them together and crushes them in the mortar of its conscience. It cooks them, as it were, within a breast that boils up like a pot over the fire of repentance and sorrow, so that it can exclaim with the Prophet: "My heart became hot within me. As I mused the fire burned." Here then is one ointment which the sinful soul should provide at the beginning of its conversion and apply to its still smarting wounds, for the first sacrifice acceptable to God is a broken spirit.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY I

"I have spoken", he says, "with my tongue". Let us consider what he has spoken with his tongue: for it seems to me that through these things he indicates something mystical. He says therefore: "Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what is lacking to me". If, he says, thou hast made known my end to me, and hast made known to me how great is the number of my days, I shall be able through these things to know also that other thing, what is lacking to me. Or perhaps through these things this too will seem to be indicated, that just as there is some end of every art — for example, the end of building is to make a house; of ship-building, to construct a ship which can overcome the waves of the sea and bear the assaults of the winds; and of each art there is some such end, on account of which the art itself seems to have been devised: so perhaps there is a certain end of our way, or of the whole world, on account of which are done all the things that are done in our life, or on account of which the world itself was either established or subsists. Of which end the Apostle too makes mention, saying: "Then the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father". Toward which end indeed we must hasten, so that this very thing may be worth the effort, that we were created by God. And again, just as the frame of our body, small and slight from the beginning of birth, yet immediately urges and stretches toward a certain end of its stature through the increases of age, and again, just as our soul, according to that which it passes in this body, hastens first to receive a stammering speech, secondly then a clearer one, and then at last to arrive at perfect and complete discourse: in this way also our whole life is now imbued as it were stammering among men on earth: but it is consummated and arrives at its summit in the heavenly places with God. The prophet therefore desires for this reason to know his end, on account of which he was made, so that, gazing at the end and beholding his days and considering perfection, he may see how much is lacking to him toward that end to which he tends. For example, as if we should suppose someone handed over to a craft, and this man saying to his master, I wish to know what the perfection of this craft is, and to know who is the perfect smith or builder: and when he has learned this, let him inquire how much is lacking to him from that perfection, or how much he has advanced in the discipline of the craft, so that when he has known both, he may know what he has, and may recognize what is lacking to perfection; so also now the prophet prays to learn from God, that there may be made known to him his end, and what the number of his days is. In which it is not to be thought that he speaks of the bodily time and the years of this life, but he wishes to know the whole number of days, what it was in the first life, what it was in the second sojourning, what in the third. "For much", he says, "was my soul a sojourner". As if those who went out of Egypt should say: "Make known to me, O Lord, my end", which is the good land and the holy land, "and the number of my days" in which I walk, "that I may know what is lacking to me", how much remains until I arrive at the holy land of promise: so also here he wishes to know the number of the days in which he makes his journey. For we have some days indeed in this world, but some also outside this world. For one day is made by this course of the sun of our heaven, bounded by the spaces of this heaven; another day has he who merits to arrive at the ascent of the second heaven. For a far brighter day does he pass who could be caught up or arrive even to the third heaven, where he will find not only ineffable light, but will also hear words which it is not permitted a man to speak. I know also other days, whose number perhaps the prophet rightly seeks. For just as in this heaven the sun, having risen and illuminating the whole world, makes a day: so also in the heart of the righteous man, which for its constancy and firmness is rightly called the firmament of God, if the sun of righteousness, Jesus Christ our Lord, rises and illuminates it with the light of knowledge and truth, he makes a day in his heart: and the more frequently he rises and illuminates, the greater a number of such days will he reckon for himself. Worthily therefore, conscious to himself of such illumination, the prophet says: "Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what is lacking to me".
Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

It is not that he was enquiring about his own death—death is not the end of one who will rise again—but rather his enquiry concerned that end of which the apostle speaks: "Afterwards there will be the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father". … Evil will fade to nothingness, and eternal good will take its place.… That, surely, is the true end. It is not the end of one person alone, but the end of all. Why then does David say "my end"? But consider a moment who it is that is speaking. He speaks as humankind or as one representing men and sharing the same substance as they; he is one who stands for all, is in the likeness of all and is truly versed in that perfection that belongs to the consummate man.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"Lord, make me to know mine end" [Psalm 39:4]. For some things I have passed by already; and I have arrived at a certain point, and that to which I have arrived is better than that from which I have advanced to this; but yet there remains a point, which has to be left behind. For we are not to remain here, where there are trials, offenses, where we have to bear with persons who listen to us and cavil at us. "Make me to know mine end;" the end, from which I am still removed, not the course which is already before me.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY I

And he adds: "Behold, thou hast set my days as old ones". In the Greek it is written, παλαιστάς, which signifies a measure of four fingers. Wishing therefore to teach us who now in this life lead brief and very few days, he spoke this verse of which we spoke above. From which it is understood that another too could say, that Thou hast set my days one finger, as following upon the brevity of time, and another two fingers or three. But I ask whether any of men can say, that My days are ten fingers, or twenty, or even more. And because we come upon difficult passages, I would wish to inquire whether somewhere in the Scriptures we find any such thing, from which that which seems obscure could be opened up more plainly. In Isaiah I remember it is written: "Who has measured", he says, "the water with his hand, and the heaven with a span, and all the earth with his fist"? From which let whoever is the more prudent of the hearers consider, through the several passages, the differences of the measures, how the part of life which is heavenly, of those indeed who merit to be called heaven, is said to be measured with the span of God, whatever that span of God is: and of those whose life is still earthly, their life is measured with the fist of God. But to inquire now the difference of the divine fist would perhaps exceed both our speech and your hearing. Nevertheless just as there he measured the water with his hand, the heaven with a span, and all the earth with his fist, and weighed the mountains in a balance, and the hills in a scale; so also here, according to the same consequence, this measure is to be understood, since to God nothing is without measure, nothing without weight, but all things stand for him in number and measure. So too the prophet's life is both numbered and measured to God, while it is governed by the reasons of his providence.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY I

He also adds in what follows and says: "My substance is as nothing before thee". Unless he had added before thee, I should be greatly grieved, for the reason that he had said the human substance to be nothing. But now, because he said before thee, it is as if he said that in comparison indeed either with the angels or with the rest of the creatures, my substance is not abject, nor least. In short, even if we act well, and keep the commandments of the Lord, we are invited to the fellowship of the angels: "They shall be", he says, "as the angels of God in heaven". But in comparison with God, even if I be Peter, against whom the gates of hell shall not prevail, my substance before him is nothing. And he used sufficiently the proper term of nature. For all is nothing, however great it be, whatever is out of nothing, for he alone is the one who is, and who always is. But our substance is as nothing before him: inasmuch as it was procreated by him out of nothing.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY I

But in what follows, as if explaining this very thing which he said, that "my substance is as nothing before thee", he added and says: "Nevertheless the whole is vanity, every living man". How do you take "living"? If indeed we think true life to be vanity, why do we labor? But see whether perhaps this which he says, every living man, is to be taken of this present life, as it is written, and we shall prove it by testimonies. For all things that are in this life among men are vain, even if Moses be in this life, for he too knows in part, and prophesies in part, and sees through a mirror and in an enigma, and knows a shadow, and is taught figures, and does not yet see the truth, and therefore he is indeed living, but his life is vanity. And do you wish to see that it is vanity? "When that which is perfect shall have come, those things which are in part shall be destroyed". But all that is destroyed is vanity. And if whatever is in part is destroyed, if the prophets know in part, rightly is their life too called vanity; but the inferior things are destroyed when those which are better and perfect have come, and by this they are proved to be vain, in that as being in part and imperfect they are destroyed. "The whole therefore is vanity, every living man". But that this sentence is to be taken of this life, hear Ecclesiastes testifying and saying: "I praised all who have died above all who live, whoever they are that live even until now, and good above these two is he who has not yet been born". He praises therefore the dead more than the living, because those have at least this much of gain, that they are freed from the bonds of this body, and are no longer clothed with flesh and skins, nor inserted into bones and sinews, nor any longer subject to the necessity of the body. If therefore you have understood what it is to live in the flesh, even if one be Moses, or whoever he is, this life is troublesome to him. For she is not released from corruption, who is surrounded by a mortal and earthly body. See therefore that the whole is vanity, every living man; let us despise this vain life, and hasten to the holy and blessed and true life, and let us tend toward it with soul and mind, all vanity being shaken off. Nor let us call sweet this light which we now use. For this those men say, who are ignorant of the sweetness of the true light, but have not perceived even any first tokens of the true light, nor do they know that an angelic life is to be hoped for by the soul, when they shall have escaped from the vanity of this life. Whence we too who believe these things, let us now be transferred in mind and faith to heaven, and walking on earth let us have our conversation in the heavens, that there may be our treasure, where our heart also is, and that we may merit to attain the heavenly kingdom, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom is glory and power and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

God, who knows precisely the allotted days of each one of us, regards nothing as immeasurable. His knowledge embraces the measure of all things. To him nothing is beyond his understanding, nothing is unweighed, nothing is unmeasured, nothing is unnumbered. He says, "The very hairs of your head have been numbered." … We know that God is said to have measured the heavens with the palm of his hand22—the palm, from thumb to little finger, being the span by which a thing is measured and its length ascertained. Those who accept this reading understand that our days are measured or numbered, and in that sense they are short. However, the all-knowing God has measured, as we said above, and fully comprehends the very heavens.… The prophet's days are not short but great, for God has measured them with the same palm as that with which he measured the heavens.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"Behold, thou hast made my days old" (ver. 5). For these days are "waxing old." I long for new days "that never shall wax old," that I may say, "Old things have passed away; behold, things are become new." Already new in hope; then in reality. For though, in hope and in faith, made new already, how much do we even now do after our old nature! For we are not so completely "clothed upon" with Christ, as not to bear about with us anything derived from Adam. Observe that Adam is "waxing old" within us, and Christ is being "renewed" in us. "Though our outward man is perishing, yet is our inward man being renewed day by day." Therefore, while we fix our thoughts on sin, on mortality, on time, that is hastening by, on sorrow, and toil, and labour, on stages of life following each other in succession, and continuing not, passing on insensibly from infancy even to old age; whilst, I say, we fix our eyes on these things, let us see here "the old man," the "day that is waxing old;" the Song that is out of date; the Old Testament; when however we turn to the inner man, to those things that are to be renewed in place of these which are to be changed, let us find the "new man," the "new day," the "new song," the "New Testament;" and that "newness," let us so love, as to have no fears of its "waxing old."... This man, therefore, who is hasting forward to those things which are new, and "reaching forward to those things which are before," says, "Lord, make me to know mine end, and the number of my days, which really is, that I may know what is wanting unto me." See he still drags with him Adam; and even so he is hasting unto Christ. "Behold," saith he, "thou hast made my days old." It is those days that are derived from Adam, those days, I say, that thou hast made old. They are waxing old day by day: and so waxing old, as to be at some day or other consumed also. "And my substance is as nothing before Thee." "Before Thee, O Lord, my substance is as nothing." "Before Thee;" who seest this; and I too, when I see it, see it only when "before Thee."

When "before men" I see it not. For what shall I say? What words shall I use to show, that which I now am is nothing in comparison of That which truly "Is"? But it is within that it is said; it is within that it is felt, so far as it is felt. "Before Thee, O Lord," where Thine eyes are; and not where the eyes of men are. And where Thine eyes are, what is the state of things? "That which I am is as nothing."

"But, verily, every man living is altogether vanity." "But, verily." For what was he saying above? Behold, I have already "leaped beyond" all mortal things, and despised things below, have trampled under foot the things of earth, have soared upwards to the delights of the law of the Lord, I have been afloat in the dispensation of the Lord, have yearned for that "End" which Itself is to know no end, have yearned for the number of my days that truly "is," because the number of days like these hath no real being. Behold, I am already such a one as this; I have already overleaped so much; I am longing for those things which abide. "But verily," in the state in which I am here, so long as I am here, so long as I am in this world, so long as I bear mortal flesh, so long as the life of man on earth is a trial, so long as I sigh among causes of offence, as long as while I "stand" I am in "fear lest I fall," as long as both my good and my ill hangs in uncertainty, "every man living is altogether vanity."...
Sermon 60

The life of mortals is a hard cause. What else is it to be born here, except to enter into a laborious life? Of the greater future labor, the very crying of the infant is a witness. From this troublesome banquet no one excuses himself. We must drink what Adam has offered. We were made by the hands of truth, but because of sin, we were cast into days of vanity. We were made in the image of God, but we wore it down through the transgression of sin. Therefore, the psalm admonishes us about how we were made, and to where we have arrived.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"Although man walks about in an image". An image is necessarily the image of something. For Holy Scripture too, when it names an image, sometimes indeed defines it and says whose image it is, but sometimes sets down "image" without any qualification. Thus, concerning the Savior, when it says "who is the image", it did not keep silent whose image he is, but added, saying: "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature". And again, when it teaches us about the diverse images, and that each single person bears some image, it says: "As we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear the image of the heavenly". With a qualification—either "of the earthly" or "of the heavenly"—it named the image. But elsewhere it speaks without any qualification, just as in this place it says: "Although man walks about in an image". But in the image of what? Of God, or in the image of the earthly, or in the image of the heavenly? How am I to know in this what it is that divine Scripture wishes to teach us, which says without any qualification: "Although man walks about in an image (I know not whose)"? For if indeed it were speaking of the righteous alone, it would without doubt have said: Although man walks about in the image of the heavenly. Or if it were speaking of sinners only, it would surely have said: Man walks about in the image of the earthly. But since it is pronounced generally concerning all mortals—of whom some bear the image of the heavenly, namely all who live according to the law of God, and others bear the image of the earthly, who live according to the flesh—therefore it necessarily kept silent about the specific designation of the image, and set forth a general judgment concerning all men, that every man walks about in an image. It is now for you to examine and search out from each one's faith and works, from his manner of life and deeds, from his thoughts and words, and to consider whether he walks about in the image of the heavenly or in the image of the earthly. If you are merciful as your heavenly Father is merciful, without doubt the image of the heavenly Father is in you. If you do good not only to your friends but even to your enemies, repaying good for evil, just as the heavenly Father "makes his sun to rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust", the image of the heavenly is in you. And if you are perfect in all things, as your heavenly Father is perfect, the image of the heavenly is in you. And again, if you are not an imitator of Christ nor of the apostle Paul, who says: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ", but are an imitator of the works of the devil, who was a murderer from the beginning; and if you are wise in earthly things, and speak earthly things, and your treasure and your heart are on the earth, you bear the image of the earthly. But since we have come upon these places in which discussion has been stirred up concerning the image, it seems necessary to bring forward into the midst also that verse of the psalm in which it is written concerning sinners: "Lord, in your city you will bring their image to nothing". It is established therefore that God brings the image of sinners in his city to nothing; but the image of the righteous he without doubt guards and preserves. This, then, is the image of the earthly, that is, of sinners, which God will bring to nothing in his city; that is, if anyone departs from this world and carries with him the image of the earthly, on account of an image of this kind he will be brought to nothing in that city of God, nor will he obtain a portion among the citizens of that heavenly city, whoever carries back no insignia of the heavenly image.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

But this verse seems to me to contain also another mystery: that the life and manner of living in this world is a kind of imaginary thing and an image, while the future one will not be imaginary but true; and this is what is meant, that each person has an image of virtue, yet does not properly and sincerely live in the virtue itself. Now what we say is of this sort: Wisdom and knowledge are a great part of the virtues; but in the present life, if anyone thinks he has known, he has not yet known as he ought to know, for he who knows, knows in a riddle. Therefore we walk about in an image of knowledge and not in knowledge itself, through which one knows face to face. So likewise we walk about in the image of wisdom, and not yet in wisdom itself, because we do not yet behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. The same things I dare to say concerning the righteousness of God, that we walk about in an image of righteousness, and do not yet proceed in that righteousness which is face to face. For human nature, clothed with skin and flesh, set within bones and sinews, will not be able to grasp righteousness itself bare, nor to bear and endure its sincere truth according to the power and strength of its nature. For Christ himself is the nature of the virtues: he himself is the righteousness which did not come to the human race in the fullness of its splendor, because Jesus Christ emptied himself of the form of God, that he might take the form of a servant. And indeed if the discourse of Scripture were speaking of the Jews alone, it would perhaps have said: Although man walks about in a shadow; but because, as I judge, the discourse is about those who are better than were those who lived according to the shadow of the law, therefore it is written: "Although man walks about in an image". This will come more clearly to understanding from the words of the apostle Paul, who designates three kinds of properties in the law, speaking of a shadow and an image and the truth; for he says: "For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things, can never by the same sacrifices which they offer unceasingly year by year make perfect those who draw near". Therefore the law has a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things, thus showing that the image of the things is other than what is designated by that shadow. And if anyone can perceive that that observance of the Jewish worship, and that temple, did not have an image but a shadow, let him see also that the altar and the goats and the calves that are offered—that all these are a shadow, concerning which it is written: "A shadow upon the earth". But if anyone comes from the shadow to the image of the things, and sees the coming of Christ made in the flesh, let him see him as high priest, offering indeed even now sacrifices to the Father, and hereafter about to offer them; and let him understand that all these are images of spiritual things, and that by bodily services heavenly things are designated. Therefore that is called an image which is received for the present, and which human nature can behold. If you can penetrate the heavens with mind and spirit, and follow Jesus who penetrated the heavens, and now stands before the countenance of God on our behalf, there you will find those good things whose shadow the law had, and whose image Christ showed in the flesh, which have been prepared for the blessed, which neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man. When you have seen these, you will understand that he who walks about in them, and continues in the desire and longing for them, this one no longer walks about in an image, but already in the truth itself. "Yet man walks about in an image". Let us therefore repeat that discourse which the Apostle spoke, in which he designated two general images, one indeed earthly, but the other heavenly, and let us compare with this the words "Although man walks about in an image"; and let us divide this thing that has been said generally into many kinds, so that when the discourse is divided through each part and examined, what lies hidden within may become clear. Now this is what we say: Every hostile power, and every divine virtue which lends aid to those who desire to obtain salvation—each of these expresses certain images in the soul of those who present themselves by diverse pursuits to be a receptacle of them. For example, as we said above, all men indeed bear either the image of the heavenly or of the earthly, but even within these very things there is much diversity. For instance, every sinner bears the image of the earthly, but not everyone in the same way: the murderer and the liar, or the adulterer and the reviler, or the corrupter of boys and the thief do not equally bear the image of the earthly—although all these bear the image of the earthly, yet there is much difference among them according to the diversity of sin. According to these diversities, then, of the image of the earthly, contemplate also the diversity of the image of the heavenly, and behold Paul bearing the image of the heavenly, and Timothy. And what then? Do we think that the image of the heavenly was in Timothy in the same way as in Paul? Did the image of Paul have nothing more, nothing more excellent beyond the image of Timothy? I judge that, according to that in which Paul preceded Timothy in the merits of his life, in the power of his word, in the greatness of soul of his purpose, so also in him there shone forth a greater and more splendid image of the heavenly—such an image as Christ formed in him, when he spoke in him; and another and, as I judge, far inferior image was formed in him by the one who said: "And the angel who was speaking in me said". And thus, searching through each thing even within yourself, you will find a diversity of image, whether earthly in sinners or heavenly in the saints. Everything, therefore, that is done by us through each hour or moment fashions some image; and therefore we ought to examine our acts through each detail, and to test ourselves in this deed and in that word, whether a heavenly or an earthly image is depicted in our soul. But it will not seem useless to remind you also of this, that many in this world have perished on account of images of evil kings—or rather of tyrants—for this alone, that tyrannical images were found in their possession, and this alone sufficed for their condemnation. Let each one of you therefore now search himself, and review the secret places of his heart, and diligently inquire what images he bears there. If you are found to have there the forms of the devil and the image of Satan, what refuge of life will there be for you, who will have mercy on you, when from the innermost chamber of your heart a tyrannical image will be brought forth? But if you wish that I designate for you images of this kind by their species, hear. Anger is a tyrannical image; avarice, deceit, pride, arrogance, worldly glories, envies, drunkenness, carousings, and things like these. And if you do not more quickly cast these out of your house, if you do not draw off and scrape away from your senses every disguise of this most wicked painting, and wipe off every figment of this poisoned color, these very images will make you perish. This concerning that which is written: "Man walks about in an image".
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

There follows: "He treasures up, and knows not for whom he gathers these things". For it was necessary to inquire what those things are that are treasured up while it is unknown for whom they are gathered, and what those things are that are gathered while it is not unknown for whom they remain.
Commentary on Ezekiel

We too can point out idols painted on the walls of our temple, when we are subject to all vices and paint in our heart the consciousness of sins and various images, of which it is said in the psalm too: O Lord, in your city you will scatter their image, and in another place: Yet man walks about in an image. That is, there is no one among men who does not have some image, whether of holiness or of sin; for which reason it is said of the furious and the wrathful: Their fury is after the likeness of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voices of the charmers; and of wicked men: Generation of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come?; and of the shifty and deceitful: Go, tell this fox; and of lovers of women: They have become to me horses mad for females; each one neighed after his neighbor's wife; and also of the brutish and senseless: Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding; and again: With bit and bridle bind fast their jaws, who do not draw near to you; and many things of this kind.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"Albeit man walketh in the Image" [Psalm 39:6]. In what "Image," save that of Him who said, "Let Us make man in Our Image, after Our Likeness." "Albeit man walks in the Image." For the reason he says "albeit," is, that this is some great thing. And this "albeit" is followed by "nevertheless," that the "albeit" which you have already heard, should relate to what is beyond the sun; but this "nevertheless," which is to follow, to what is "under the sun," and that the one should relate to the Truth, the other to "vanity." "Albeit," then, "that man walketh in the Image, nevertheless he is disquieted in vain." Hear the cause of his "disquieting," and see if it be not a vain one; that thou mayest trample it under foot, that thou mayest "leap beyond it," and mayest dwell on high, where that "vanity" is not. What "vanity" is that? "He heapeth up riches, and knoweth not for whom he may be gathering them together." O infatuated vanity! "Blessed is the man that maketh the Lord his trust, and hath not respected vanities, nor lying deceits." To you indeed, O covetous man, to you I seem to be out of my senses, these words appear to you to be "old wives' tales." For you, a man of great judgment, and of great prudence, to be sure, are daily devising methods of acquiring money, by traffic, by agriculture, by eloquence perhaps, by making yourself learned in the law, by warfare, perhaps you even add that of usury. Like a shrewd man as you are, you leave nothing untried, whereby you may pile coin on coin; and may store it up more carefully in a place of secrecy. You plunder others; you guard against the plunderer; you are afraid lest you should yourself suffer the wrong, that you yourself do; and even what you do suffer, does not correct you. ...Examine your own heart, and that prudence of yours, which leads you to deride me, to think me out of my senses for saying these things: and tell me now, "You are heaping up treasures; for whom are you gathering them together?" I see what you would tell me; as if what you would say had not occurred to the person described here; you will say, I am keeping them for my children? This is the voice of parental affection; the excuse of injustice. "I am keeping them" (you say) "for my children." So then you are keeping them for your children, are you? Did not Idithun then know this? Assuredly he did; but he reckoned it one of the things of the "old days," that have waxed old, and therefore he despised it: because he was hastening on to the new "days."...

For He, "by whom all things were made," hath built "mansions" for all of us: thither He would have that which we have go before us; that we may not lose it on earth. When, however, you have kept them on earth, tell me for whom you are to "gather them together"? You have children: add one more to their number; and give something to Christ also. "He is disquieted in vain."
Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 80

The soul is great in that it is capable of eternal things, and upright in that it desires heavenly things: the soul which does not seek or savor the things that are above, but the things that are upon the earth, is plainly not upright, but crooked, even though on account of this it does not cease to be great, remaining as it does even so capable of eternity. For it will never at any time not be capable of eternity, even if it never shall have been actually possessing it, so that it may be as it is written: "Surely man passes through as an image"; yet only in part, so that the eminence of the Word may be apparent from its very wholeness. For in what respect could the Word fall from being great or upright, since it so possesses these things that it is what it has? Or it is in part for this reason: lest, if the soul were deprived of the whole, no hope of salvation would remain. For if it should cease to be great, it would also cease to be capable. For the greatness of the soul, as I said, is estimated from its capacity. But what could it hope for, of which it were not capable?

And so through the greatness which it retains even when uprightness is lost, man passes through as an image, limping as it were on one foot, and become an alien son. For of such I believe it was said: "The alien sons have lied to me, the alien sons have grown old, and they have limped from their paths." Fittingly they are called alien sons: for sons, on account of the greatness they have retained; aliens, on account of the uprightness they have lost. Nor would he have said "they limped," but rather "they fell," or something similar, if men had entirely put off the image. But as things stand, according to greatness indeed man passes through as an image; but as far as uprightness is concerned, as one limping, he is troubled and cast down from the image, Scripture speaking thus: "Surely man passes through as an image; but indeed he is troubled in vain." In vain altogether: for it follows: "He heaps up treasure, and knows not for whom he gathers it." Why does he not know, unless because, bending himself down to these lowest and earthly things, he heaps up earth for himself? Assuredly he does not know, concerning those things which he commits to the earth, for whom he gathers them: whether for the moth that destroys, or for the thief that digs through; for the enemy that plunders, or for the fire that devours.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 19:157
We will have to say that if we give in to troubles, we do not believe in him insofar as he is endurance; and if we are weak, we have not believed in him insofar as he is strength.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

There follows: "And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?" As Christ is our wisdom, and Christ is righteousness, according to what is written: "Who was made wisdom for us from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption"; so also our expectation, that is, our patience, is Christ. Therefore let not the wise man glory in wisdom, nor the strong in his strength, because we have all things in Christ. And now therefore what is my expectation, that is, my patience? The Lord. "And my substance is from you". If I have a substance of spiritual riches, it is from God; "for God breathed into the face of man the breath of life, and man was made into a living soul".
Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

Our hope and our patience is Christ; he is our redemption; he is our expectation.… Look on us, Lord, when you come in judgment; let your mercy look on us.… In the power of your mercy lies the substance of our soul and life. We must not fear physical death; rather, we should fear him who can save or destroy our soul. Our soul's substance is that virtue that God has poured into hearts made in the image of himself.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"And now" [Psalm 39:7]. "And now," saith this Idithun,-looking back on a certain "vain" show, and looking up to a certain Truth, standing midway where he has something beyond him, and something also behind him, having below him the place from which he took his spring, having above him that toward which he has stretched forth;-"And now," when I have "over-leaped" some things, when I have trampled many things under foot, when I am no longer captivated by things temporal; even now, I am not perfect, "I have not yet apprehended." "For it is by hope that we are saved; but hope that is seen is not hope; for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it." Therefore he says: "And now what wait I for? Is it not for the Lord?" He is my expectation, who hath given me all those things, that I might despise them. He will give unto me Himself also, even He who is above all, and "by whom all things were made," and by whom I was made amongst all; even He, the Lord, is my Expectation! You see Idithun, brethren, you see in what way he waiteth for Him! Let no man therefore call himself perfect here; he deceives and imposes upon himself; he is beguiling himself, he cannot have perfection here, and what avails it that he should lose humility?...

"And my substance is ever before Thee." Already advancing, already tending towards Him, and to some extent already beginning to "be," still (he says ) "my substance is ever before Thee." Now that other substance is also before men. You have gold, silver, slaves, estates, trees, cattle, servants. These things are visible even to men. There is a certain "substance that is ever before Thee."
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"From all my iniquities deliver me". He necessarily added "from all", so that of course no iniquity may hold and constrain us. But let us consider how God delivers from iniquities. If, repenting for our evil deeds, we turn to God, God, receiving our conversion from us, grants absolution of iniquities according to the measure of the conversion. For to whom more is remitted, loves more; and therefore it is said of that woman that "much was remitted to her, because she loved much". According to the measure of the repentance, then, the quantity of remission is regulated; let us not deceive ourselves, thinking that these things are dispensed by no rules, by no judgments. For I think that he who has fulfilled all righteousnesses washes away all iniquities; but he who has worked few, or some part of righteousness, dissolves some part of his iniquities; and he who has borne perfect and entire repentance for all his evils, so that he now offers a pure heart to God, this one washes away at once every stain of his sins; but if he has repented in part, he has also in part now merited absolution. Knowing these things, then, and that God delivers some indeed from all their iniquities, while he frees others from some iniquities, the prophet, confident, I think, that he had done those things by which he would be worthy to be delivered from all iniquities, says boldly to the Lord: "From all my iniquities deliver me".
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"You have made me a reproach to the foolish". As long as we have sins, it is necessary that we be reproached by the foolish one and our accuser, the devil; and if our sins are found not to be blotted out, but written in us by the pen of the devil, through these very things which we have done the enemy will reproach us. For just as all good things are said to be written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, so all evil things are written down with the ink and pen of the devil. On account of which our Lord and Savior blotted out the handwriting of our sins, which was written against us with the devil's endorsement, just as he had also foretold before through the prophet who said: "Behold, I blot out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist, and I will no longer remember them". Therefore, that we may not be reproached by the foolish one, let us turn ourselves away from all our iniquities, lest, censuring in us the stains of sins—that is, the insignia of his own will—he reproach us and say: Behold, this man was called a Christian, and was sealed with the sign of Christ on his forehead, but he bore my wills and my handwritings in his heart. Behold, this man who renounced me and my works in baptism has again inserted himself into my works and obeyed my laws. Freed therefore from all iniquities, let us take care that on the day of judgment we do not succumb to reproaches of this kind from the foolish devil.
Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

It is not merely one lapse that he is confessing, for he prays to be forgiven all his iniquities. He knows that without God's forgiveness no one can be saved. For we were born in sin. We have inherited a stain. Our human condition has a congenital tendency to sin.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"Deliver me from all my transgressions" [Psalm 39:8]. I have "over-leaped" a great deal of ground, a very great deal of ground already; but, "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the Truth is not in us." I have "over-leaped" a great deal: but still do I "beat my breast," and say, "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Thou therefore art "my expectation!" my "End." For "Christ is the end of the Law unto righteousness, unto every man that believeth." From all mine offences: not only from those, that I may not relapse into those which I have already "over-leaped;" but from all, without exception, of those on account of which I now beat my breast, and say, "Forgive us our debts." "Deliver me from all mine offences:" me being thus minded, and holding fast what the Apostle said, "As many of us as be perfect, let us be thus minded." For at the time that he said that he was not "already perfect," he then immediately goes on and says, "As many of us as be perfect, let us be thus minded."... Art thou then, O Apostle, not perfect, and are we perfect? But hath it escaped you, that he did just now call himself "perfect"? For he does not say, "As many of you as are perfect, be ye thus minded;" but "As many of us as be perfect, let us be thus minded;" after having said a little before, "Not that I have already attained; either am already perfect." In no other way then can you be perfect in this life, than by knowing that you cannot be perfect in this life. This then will be your perfection, so to have "over-leaped" some things, as to have still some point to which you are hastening on: so as to have something remaining, to which you will have to leap on, when everything else has been passed by. It is such faith as this that is secure; for whoever thinks that he has already attained, is "exalting himself," so as to be "abused" hereafter. ...
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth, because it is you who did it". This too we have already expounded above, when we treated that verse which says: "While the sinner stands against me, I was struck dumb and was humbled and kept silence from good things". For it is good that at the time when weapons—whether of disparagements, or of insults, or of reproaches—are hurled against us, we should remember this verse which says: "I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth, because it is you who did it". This indeed seems to need inquiry: what is it that he said, "It is you who did it", and yet did not add what he did. But the very order teaches us, since it describes as a kind of contest between us and the sinner who stands against us; and that it indicates that God did this very thing, that is, that for the sake of our exercise and progress God made these struggles. Therefore for this reason I will remember, that you made these struggles and you prepared for us these exercises of patience. For when he provoked me to wrath, when he assailed me with insults, that I might not overstep the bounds of patience and utter from my lips some word that would not please you, "I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth". But if I am able to accomplish something greater according to the precepts of Paul, I will not only be struck dumb and not open my mouth, but even when I am cursed, I will bless, and when I am blasphemed, I will entreat.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"I became dumb; and I opened not my mouth" [Psalm 39:9]. But it was to guard against "the foolish man," that "I became dumb, and opened not my mouth." For to whom should I tell what is going on within me? "For I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me; for He will speak peace unto His people." But "There is no peace," says the Lord, "to the wicked." [Isaiah 48:22] "I was dumb, and opened not my mouth; because it is Thou that made me." Was this the reason that you opened not your mouth, "because God made you"? That is strange; for did not God make your mouth, that you should speak? "He that planted the ear, does He not hear? He that formed the eye, does He not see?" God has given you a mouth to speak with; and do you say, "I was dumb, and opened not my mouth, because You made me"? Or does the clause, "Because You made me," belong to the verse that follows?
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"Remove your plagues from me; from the strength of your hand I have fainted". What the Latin translators rendered "plagues," in the Greek codices is written "scourges," so that it is: "Remove your scourges from me". This one seems, of course, to say when he is set as it were under the correction of scourges, when, like a man, he is corrected for his sins, or scourged that he may be amended. Just as that also is understood by very many which is written: "Son, do not grow weary of the discipline of God, nor faint when you are rebuked by him. For whom God loves, he corrects, and scourges every son whom he receives". Whenever, therefore, anyone is rebuked with corrections of this kind, he seems fittingly to say: "Remove your scourges from me. From the strength of your hand I have fainted". But that also seems fittingly to be applied which is written: "In rebukes on account of iniquity you have corrected"—or "instructed"—"a man". But I know also other scourges by which we are more vehemently tormented, namely those which wisdom describes through the prophet (for indeed I call it a prophet): "Who will set scourges over my thought, and the correction of wisdom over my heart, that my ignorances which I have committed may not be spared, and that my sins may not be passed over?" Do you see how it prays that its heart be scourged for its sins, and that its thoughts be beaten? Whenever, therefore, you see yourself after sin afflicted and tormented in heart, and accused by your own thoughts; whenever you see yourself marked by your conscience, and scourged by its lashes, presume for yourself the hope of amendment and salvation. For the way of conversion is nearer to you than to those who do not even perceive that they have sinned, nor are grieved over their misdeeds, nor suffer the scourges of conscience. You therefore, if you see yourself scourged and tormented in your thoughts, and attending to the hope of salvation as near at hand, say concerning those who have indeed sinned in like manner, yet do not likewise repent for their misdeeds, that they "are not among the labors of men, and shall not be scourged with men; therefore pride has taken hold of them". You therefore, if you are tormented and afflicted in your heart, say to the Lord: "Many indeed are the scourges of sinners, but mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord". We have shown, then, that scourges are prepared for men in two ways: either perceptibly from without, when we are scourged either by illnesses, or by losses, or by diverse kinds of afflictions; or also when, from the recollection of a misdeed, we are bored through in heart by the goads of an urging conscience. To both, then, it is fitting to say: "Remove your plagues from me". But perhaps someone says: Granted that for these torments which are inflicted from without a prayer of this kind seems suitable, which begs that the torments cease—but will it seem to hinder also the goad of the heart and the regard of the mind? Measure is sought in all things; much more in scourges is measure very suitable. For if they are beyond measure, even those things which are good will harm you. And what shall I say about scourges? "Finding honey", says Solomon, "eat as much as suffices, lest perhaps, being sated, you vomit it up". But if in honey measure is useful, how much more rightly will it be sought and preserved in scourges? On account of which the Apostle too, fearing excessive scourges of the heart of the one who had transgressed and was grieving excessively, said: "Lest perhaps such a one be swallowed up by too great sorrow".
Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

The strong hand strikes as though harshly, but it is swift to heal. If it is powerful to wound, it is also powerful when it comes to applying a remedy. As the Lord says, "I will strike, and I will heal." … This hand of the Lord took from Job all that he had and gave it all back again. In fact, he greatly added to Job's store of good things, even doubling what he had before. Do not be troubled because David says he has fainted. A person can faint and rise up stronger than before. "The Lord lifts up all that fall and sets up all that are cast down." Whoever is corrected will rise up with virtue.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"Remove Your stroke away from me" [Psalm 39:10]. Because it is "Thou that hast made me," let it not be Your pleasure to destroy me utterly; scourge, so that I may be made better, not so that I faint; beat me, so that I may be beaten out to a greater length and breadth, not so that I may be ground to powder. "By the heaviness of Your hand I fainted in corrections." That is, I "fainted" while You were correcting me. And what is meant by "correcting" me? Except what follows.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"In rebukes for iniquity you have instructed a man, and you have made his soul waste away like a spider". The soul that sins becomes grosser. For such is the nature of sin, on account of which it is written: "The heart of this people has been made gross". But just as sin makes gross, so on the contrary virtue renders the soul subtle, and—if I may wring out, as it were, a novelty of wording—it wipes away and destroys everything corporeal in it, and renders it more purely incorporeal. But that the soul of the sinner grows gross, and, so to speak, becomes fleshly, is indicated by that which is written: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh". Without doubt he names as "flesh" the grosser and sinful souls. If, then, the soul grows gross, so that it becomes flesh, he teaches what remedy God prepares: "In rebukes", he says, "for iniquity you have instructed a man, and you have made his soul waste away like a spider". It is therefore the work of God to make waste away and consume whatever is of the grosser matter by which the soul is surrounded, that he may thin down and file away the prudence of the flesh, and thus at last recall the soul to a subtle understanding of heavenly and invisible things. Certain such things we find designated no less under a mystery in the prophet Ezekiel, when flesh is said to be put into a cauldron, or pot, and cooked, and it is said that they are cooked and have wasted away, or the flesh is boiled down and the broth is boiled off. These things are written in these very words, because the cauldrons or pots, kindled with flames, will receive us—into which we will be cast, we who have made our souls fleshly, or gross—if we do not first, while we are in this world, arrive through repentance at making our flesh waste away, and reducing the grossness of our soul to the subtlety of a spider. If we go forth still fleshly from here, we will be sent into those pots which are kindled with wood, or hay, or stubble, that is, with our works which we have laid upon the foundation of Christ. Such is that, as I suppose, which Jeremiah says: "I saw", he says, "a cauldron or pot burning, and its face from the face of the north". Or again when he saw a rod of nut-wood. Let us therefore inquire concerning this saying, why he showed at the same time a rod and a pot kindled with fire: so that, if indeed you accept discipline through the rod and are amended, you may have no need of the kindled pot; but if you remain undisciplined and are not amended by the rod—that is, by the word of correction, either confuted or repenting, and corrected by such a rod as Paul speaks of: "What do you wish—that I come to you with a rod, or in the love of a spirit and of gentleness?"—if, then, you are not amended by such a rod, you will be sent into the pot, and the pot will be kindled. For this reason, then, Jeremiah saw both at the same time, both the rod and the kindled pot, so that, fearing both, we may see the one from the other. This concerning that which is written: "You have made his soul waste away like a spider".
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

If, then, we turn the discourse back to the nature of that animal, from that aspect by which it unfolds a most subtle work which the eye can scarcely comprehend, the exposition which we explained above will seem apt. But if anyone refers it to that which Isaiah writes in his book, that "they have woven the web of a spider", it is to be taken otherwise: that all the things which the sinner weaves and does, you may know to be as nothing as those things which the spider weaves, though they seem varied and composed, though arranged with a certain exquisite art. How much did those rich men who were before us weave, who gathered riches by various arts and cunning devices, who sought magistracies, honors, consulships with diverse ambition—all these wove the webs of a spider. For as vain, as frivolous as is the weaving of the spider, so were all the things they did, and therefore their souls have been made to waste away like the spider's. "Yet every man is vanity". This we have already explained in the passages above.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"Thou with rebukes hast chastened man for iniquity; Thou hast made my life to consume away like a spider" (ver. 11). There is much that is discerned by this Idithun; by every one who discerns as he does; who overleaps as he does. For he says, that he has fainted in God's corrections; and would fain have the stroke removed away from him, "because it is He who made him." Let Him renew me, who also made me; let Him who created me, create me anew. But yet, Brethren, do we suppose that there was no cause for his fainting, so that he wishes to be "renewed," to be "created anew"? It is "for iniquity," saith he, "that Thou hast chastened man." All this, my having fainted, my being weak, my "crying out of the deep," all of this is because of "iniquity;" and in this Thou hast not condemned, but hast "chastened" me. "Thou hast chastened man for sin." Hear this more plainly from another Psalm: "It is good for me that Thou hast afflicted me, that I might learn Thy righteousness." I have been "afflicted," and at the same time "it is good for me;" it is at once a punishment, and an act of favour. What hath He in store for us after punishment is over, who inflicts punishment itself by way of favour? For He it is of whom it was said, "I was brought low, and He made me whole:" and, "It is good for me that Thou hast afflicted me, that I might learn Thy righteousness." "Thou chastenest man for iniquity." And that which is written, "Thou formest my grief in teaching me," could only be said unto God by one who was "leaping beyond" his fellows; "Thou formest my grief in teaching me;" Thou makest, that is to say, a lesson for me out of my sorrow. It is Thou that formest that very grief itself; Thou dost not leave it unformed, but formest it; and that grief, that has been inflicted by Thee, when formed, will be a lesson unto me, that I may be set free by Thee. For the word finges is used in the sense of "forming," as it were moulding, my grief; not in the sense of "feigning" it; in the same way that fingit is applied to the artist, in the same sense that figulus is derived from fingere. Thou therefore "hast chastened man for iniquity." I see myself in afflictions; I see myself under punishment; and I see no unrighteousness in Thee. If I therefore am under punishment, and if there is no unrighteousness with Thee, it remains that Thou must have been "chastening man for iniquity."

And by what means hast Thou "chastened" him? Tell us, O Idithun, the manner of thy chastening; tell us in what way thou hast been "chastened." "And Thou hast made my life consume like a spider." This is the chastening! What consumes away sooner than the spider? I speak of the creature itself; though what can be more liable to "consume away" than the spider's webs? Observe too how liable to decay is the creature itself. Do but set your finger lightly upon it, and it is a ruin: there is nothing at all more easily destroyed. To such a state hast Thou brought my life, by chastening me "because of iniquity." When chastening makes us weak, there is a kind of strength that would be a fault. ...It was by a kind of strength that man offended, so as to require to be corrected by weakness: for it was by a certain "pride" that he offended; so as to require to be chastened by humility. All proud persons call themselves strong men. Therefore have many "come from the East and the West," and have attained "to sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of Heaven." Wherefore was it that they so attained? Because they would not be strong. What is meant by "would not be strong"? They were afraid to presume of their own merits. They did not "go about to establish their own righteousness," that they might "submit themselves to the righteousness of God." ...Behold! you are mortal; and you bear about you a body of flesh that is corrupting away: "And ye shall fall like one of the princes. Ye shall die like men," and shall fall like the devil. What good does the remedial discipline of mortality do you? The devil is proud, as not having a mortal body, as being an angel. But as for you, who have received a mortal body, and to whom even this does no good, so as to humble you by so great weakness, you shall "fall like one of the princes." This then is the first grace of God's gift, to bring us to the confession of our infirmity, that whatever good we can do, whatever ability we have, we may be that in Him; that "He that glorieth, may glory in the Lord." "When I am weak," saith he, "then am I strong."
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"Hear my prayer, O God, and my supplication; give ear to my tears". It is fitting once again to offer prayer to God even with tears, and to be moved from the innermost recesses into supplication of the Lord, so that the mind, believing in the judgment to come, may review the recollection of its misdeeds not without tears and lamentation. Who, dissolved into tears, says to the Lord: "I pour out my prayer in your sight"? "Give ear, therefore, to my tears, and be not silent", he says, "from me"—that is, while I pray be not silent. But what then? While I am still speaking, say: Behold, I am here.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"For I am a sojourner with you, and a pilgrim, as all my fathers". Because I am a pilgrim, I am necessarily also a sojourner, for I am not as you are. For you alone are eternal, and we, as far as is found, have a beginning. But I, if I be made worthy to be with you, am nevertheless a sojourner and a pilgrim with you; because all my fathers too were sojourners and pilgrims with you; and Abraham is a pilgrim with you, because he did not always exist, but then began to exist when you willed, and so Isaac and Jacob and all the righteous.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"Hear my prayer, O Lord" (ver. 12). Whereof shall I rejoice? Whereof should I groan? I rejoice on account of what is past, I groan longing for these which are not yet come. "Hear my prayer, and give ear unto my cry. Hold not Thy peace at my tears." For do I now no longer weep, because I have already "passed by," have "left behind" so great things as these? "Do I not weep much the more?" For, "He that increaseth knowledge, increaseth sorrow." The more I long for what is not here, do I not so much the more groan for it until it comes? do I not so much the more weep until it comes?...

"For I am a sojourner with Thee." But with whom am I a "sojourner"? When I was with the devil, I was a "sojourner;" but then I had a bad host and entertainer; now, however, I am with Thee; but I am a "sojourner" still. What is meant by a sojourner? I am a "sojourner" in the place from which I am to remove; not in the place where I am to dwell for ever. The place where I am to abide for ever, should be rather called my home. In the place from which I am to remove I am a "sojourner;" but yet it is with my God that I am a sojourner, with whom I am hereafter to abide, when I have reached my home. But what home is that to which you are to remove from this estate of a sojourner? Recognise that home, of which the Apostle speaks, "We have an habitation of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the Heavens." If this house is eternal in the Heavens, when we have come to it, we shall not be sojourners any more. For how should you be a sojourner in an eternal home? But here, where the Master of the house is some day to say to you, "Remove," while you yourself know not when He will say it, be thou in readiness. And by longing for your eternal home, you will be keeping yourself in readiness for it. And be not angry with Him, because He gives thee notice to remove, when He Himself pleases. For He made no covenant with thee, nor did He bind Himself by any engagement; nor didst thou enter upon the tenancy of this house on a certain stipulation for a definite term: thou art to quit, when it is its Master's pleasure. For therefore is it that you now dwell there free of charge. "For I am a sojourner with Thee, and a stranger." Therefore it is there is my country: it is there is my home. "I am a sojourner with Thee, and a stranger." Here too is understood "with Thee." For many are strangers with the devil: but they who have already believed and are faithful, are, it is true, "strangers" as yet, because they have not yet come to that country and to that home: but still they are strangers with God. For so long as we are in the body, we are strangers from the Lord, and we desire, whether we are strangers, or abiding here, "we may be accepted with Him." I am a "sojourner with Thee; and a stranger, as all my fathers were." If then I am as all my fathers were, shall I say that I will not remove, when they have removed? Am I to lodge here on other terms, than those on which they lodged here also?...
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 39, HOMILY II

"Give me remission that I may be refreshed before I depart, and shall be no more, for I am a sojourner": as long as I am with you, so long I am; but if I go forth from you, I have lost even this very thing that I am, and I shall be as one who is not. Thus for this reason he says concerning sinners: "And they shall be as those who are not". And elsewhere: "Who called the things that are not". "Give me remission that I may be refreshed before I depart, and shall be no more". It must be known, nevertheless, that it is within us either to be or not to be. As long as we cleave to God and are joined to him who truly is, we too are. But if we depart from him and do not cleave to our God, we fall by vice into the contrary. Not, therefore, through this is the substantial destruction of the soul designated, but it is said "not to be" when it does not remain in him who truly and always is, from whom he himself is. Therefore for this reason the prophetic word too exhorts us, saying: "After the Lord our God we shall go, and to him we shall cleave". But let us ourselves also say: "My soul has cleaved after you", in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom is honor and glory unto the ages of ages. Amen.
Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

Forgive me, so that I need no longer be a pilgrim and a wayfarer. Forgive me so that I may be called home from exile. If you forgive me, before I go from this place, I shall no longer be an exile and a pilgrim. Once you will have forgiven me, I will no longer be in foreign parts. I shall be a fellow citizen of your saints; I shall be with my ancestors, who were pilgrims before me and are now truly citizens. I shall be a member of God's household. I shall not dread punishment but shall merit grace through our Lord Jesus; with whom, Lord God, be praise to you, and honor and glory forever; now and always and for ages of ages. Amen.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'When I make you, O Tyre, a city desolate forever, as are other cities that are not inhabited at all, and bring up the deep upon you, and many waters, or boundless multitudes of enemies, cover you — or certainly, because he is speaking to an island and to a city set on an island, he τροπικῶς [figuratively] compares the throng of adversaries to the waves of the deep —, and drag you down, with those who go down into the pit or into the ditch, to those who are in hell — of whom we also read in the Psalms: They shall go into the lower parts of the earth and shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be portions for foxes —, to the everlasting people, where there is weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth, and set you in the uttermost land, in which the ancient dragon has been placed, and like the ancient wastes and deserts, where there is no remembrance of good things but punishments are everlasting, and do not cause you to be raised up in the land of the living — of which it is written: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land, and in another place: I will please the Lord in the region of the living —, then you will be reduced to nothing, or you will perish forever, and you shall be no more', according to what is written in another psalm: Spare me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and shall be no more: not that he who is in everlasting punishments ceases to be, but that he who does not live to God is said in the holy Scriptures not to subsist. Hence Esther too, speaking against idols: Do not hand over, she says, your scepter to those who are not: surely those to whom she begs that it not be handed over existed, but they were not, to God, since they had ceased to be to the virtues and to the living God.
Exposition on Psalm 39

"Grant me some remission, that I may be refreshed before I go hence" (ver. 13). Consider well, Idithun, consider what knots those are which thou wouldest have "loosed" unto thee, that thou mightest be "refreshed before thou goest hence." For thou hast certain fever-heats from which thou wouldest fain be refreshed, and thou sayest, "that I may be refreshed," and "grant me a remission." What should He remit, or loosen unto thee, save that difficulty under which, and in consequence of which, thou sayest, "Forgive us our debts. Grant me a remission before I go hence, and be no more." Set me free from my sins, "before I go hence," that I may not go hence with my sins. Remit them unto me, that I may be set at rest in my conscience, that it may be disburthened of its feverish anxiety, the anxiety with which "I am sorry for my sin. Grant me a remission, that I may be refreshed" (before everything else), "before I go hence, and be no more." For if thou grantest me not a "remission, that I may be refreshed," I shall "go and be no more." "Before I go" thither, where if I go, I shall thenceforth "be no more. Grant me a remission, that I may be refreshed." A question has suggested itself, how he will be no more. ...What is meant then by "shall be no more," unless Idithun is alluding to what is true "being," and what is not true "being." For he was beholding with the mind, with which he could do so, with the "mind's eye," by which he was able to behold it, that end, which he had desired to have shown unto him, saying, "Lord, make me to know mine end." He was beholding "the number of his days, which truly is;" and he observed that all that is below, in comparison of that true being, has no true being. For those things are permanent; these are subject to change; mortal, and frail, and the eternal suffering, though full of corruption, is for this very reason not to be ended, that it may ever be being ended without end. He alluded therefore to that realm of bliss, to the happy country, to the happy home, where the Saints are partakers of eternal Life, and of Truth unchangeable; and he feared to "go" where that is not, where there is no true being; longing to be there, where "Being" in the highest sense is! It is on account of this contrast then, while standing midway between them, he says, "Grant me a remission, that I may be refreshed before I go hence and be no more." For if Thou "grantest me not a remission" of my sins, I shall go from Thee unto all eternity! And from whom shall I go to all eternity? From Him who said, I Am He that Am: from Him who said, "Say unto the children of Israel, I Am hath sent me unto you." He then who goes from Him, in the contrary direction, goes to non-existence. ...

n: Psalm. Protestants intimate that this was not in the Hebrew; but we find mizmor, "canticle," which is equivalent. (Haydock) --- David speaks of his own restoration to health as a figure of Jesus Christ, who is principally intended, Hebrews x. 7. The end of the psalm is nearly the same with the 69th. (Calmet) --- Some arbitrarily (Berthier) explain the words with relation to the revolt of Absalom. (Bossuet) --- Others think it may refer to the captives, (Ven. Bede) to Daniel, or Jeremias, rescued from prison. See Theodoret, who explains it of men waiting for the general resurrection. It may express the sentiments of the Church, when the persecutions ceased. (Euthymius) --- Christ sometimes speaks in his own name, and sometimes in that of his members. (St. Ambrose; St. Augustine) (Calmet) --- It is certain that David had Christ in view; and if he alludes to himself, it is only as the figure of him. (Berthier)
Expectation, or patience. (Haydock) --- God has, at last, granted my request.

Misery. Hebrew, "confusion," (Berthier) or "noise," (St. Jerome; Haydock) from the greatest danger. (Theodoret) --- Dregs. Mud, Jeremias xxxviii. 6. St. Augustine, &c., explain this of the Christian saved by faith from the sink of his sins. (Calmet)

New. Excellent. (Haydock) --- I was before uttering complaints, now I give thanks with joy, for my health and conversion. (Calmet) --- Song. Hebrew, "Praise." The penitent changes his language, which is no longer understood by worldlings. (Berthier) --- Many. St. Augustine reads, the just, who take part in the welfare of their brethren, (Psalm xxxi. 11.) while the wicked are filled with alarm, at the ways of God; who humbles or exalts people as he pleases. (Calmet)
Vanities. Hebrew, "the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies." (Protestants) (Haydock) --- All the world is vanity, (Psalm xxxviii. 6., &c.; Calmet) though idolatry may be here meant. (St. Cyril)

Thoughts, or designs, "over us," as Hebrew adds. No one can fathom the counsels of the Lord. It is folly, therefore, to attack his mysteries. (Haydock) --- Like. Protestants, "and thy thoughts which are to usward, they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee." Literally, non ordinare apud te. (Montanus) (Haydock) --- But haroc means also æquiparare, which corresponds with the Vulgate. (Berthier) --- Syriac, "none is comparable to thee." (Calmet) --- Number. Christ and his apostles preached, so that many followed their doctrine. (Worthington) --- David also had many witnesses of his gratitude. They crowded round him. Some would improperly make multiplicati sunt, agree with mirabilia, dialogismois, which is in the masculine. (Berthier) --- "I find no order before thee; if I would declare and number, they are more (wonders) than can be counted." (St. Jerome) (Haydock) --- I am at a loss how to express myself, and must be content with the interior sentiments of gratitude. See Psalm lxx. 15. (Calmet)

Sacrifice and oblation. Neither bloody nor unbloody sacrifices of the law will do. (Menochius) --- Pierced ears. Septuagint and St. Paul read, a body thou hast fitted to me, Hebrews x. 5. (Haydock) --- Nobilius mentions, that he found the reading of the Vulgate in one Greek manuscript in Eusebius, &c. --- The Arabic has both. "Thou hast prepared a body for me, and opened my ears." (Calmet) --- Both are, in effect, of divine authority. The version adopted by St. Paul, cannot be rejected, no more than the Hebrew confirmed by the Vulgate. James Pierce asserts, that the Hebrew is incorrect, oznaim being put for az zip, "then a body," as the letters are not unlike. The dissertation is ingenious: the author is, however, suspected of Socinianism. We know not the reason why the Vulgate here abandons the Septuagint. The sense is much the same; the prophet noticing the entire obedience of the Messias, (Berthier) and the apostle comprising his whole person. (Menochius) --- His body was miraculous, (Haydock) and the incarnation the work of God. (Calmet) --- Nothing could come up to his submission. "Thou has dug ears for me," (St. Jerome; Haydock) alluding to the custom of making slaves for ever, (Exodus xxi. 5.) or "thou hast fitted, (Calmet) opened, (Protestants) my ears," enabling me to hear, and to obey. (Haydock) --- The sacrifice of Christ was never interrupted, from the first moment of his incarnation. (Calmet) --- He was always doing the will of his Father. (Haydock) --- This sacrifice is the most essential. God rejected all such as were destitute of this condition, or were not offered by people determined to observe the whole law, 1 Kings xv. 22., Isaias i. 11., and Jeremias vii. 22. (Porphyrius, Abs. ii.) (Calmet) --- No sacrifice of the Old Testament was sufficient to satisfy God's justice for sin. Christ, by the ear of obedience, performed the redemption of man by his death, as was determined from eternity. See Hebrews x. (Worthington) --- And is omitted in the Latin version of St. Paul, holocautomata pro peccato, inadvertently, or rather to intimate, that he was speaking of the holocaust of expiation, Hebrews x. 6, 8., and xiii. 11., and Leviticus xvi. 27. (Berthier) --- St. Augustine also admits only one species of sacrifice, "holocausts likewise for sin." But others distinguish them from the victims designed to expiate the sins of individuals, (Leviticus v., &c.) of which the prophet also speaks. (Calmet)

Head, or beginning, (Genesis i., John i., and viii. 25.; St. Jerome, &c.) or at the commencement of this book of Psalms, (St. Augustine) or rather in the whole Bible. (Calmet) --- Kephalis denotes a volume, (Suidas) or stick, on which books were formerly rolled, being written on parchment. The Jews still observe the same custom in their synagogues. (Calmet) (Luke iv. 17, 20.) --- Hebrew, "In the volume of the book," means, in the book, (Amama) or the Bible, which is the book by excellence, where the incarnation and death of Christ, for man's redemption, are clearly specified. (Haydock) --- This is the sum of the Scriptures. (Worthington) --- They bear witness to Christ, John v. 39., and Luke xxiv. 27. (Haydock) --- The apostle uses the word capitulum, for the sum, Hebrews viii. Whatever sense be chosen, we should meditate on this head, or volume. But Christ signed, as it were, this solemn engagement, from all eternity. If we adopt the passage to David, we may translate, "I come, having on me the volume of thy Scriptures." See 4 Kings xi. 12. (Calmet)

Heart. So the Vatican Septuagint reads; while other editions have koilias, "belly." (St. Jerome, ad Sum.) --- Hebrew, "bowels." (Haydock) --- The sense is the same. (Berthier) --- I love the law so much, that I would hide it in my bowels, (Calmet) or in the most secret place. (Theodoret)

Thy, is not expressed in Hebrew or Greek, but understood. (Berthier) --- Church, in the tabernacle, (Theodoret) or rather in the Catholic Church; the propagation of which, (Haydock) and the preaching of the gospel throughout the world are foretold. (Worthington) --- The justice, or mercies of our Saviour, are every where proclaimed. (St. Jerome) (Calmet)

Thy. Some copies of the Septuagint have, my justice, as well as the Ethiopic version. (Eusebius; St. Augustine, &c.) (Calmet) --- But the Vulgate is more correct. (Berthier) --- Council. Christ conceals not his mercy and truth from the greatest and wisest congregations. He spoke boldly before Annas and Caiphas, as St. Paul did at Athens, &c. (Worthington) --- David testifies his gratitude, and invites all to praise God with him. (Calmet) --- But we must particularly learn from our Saviour, a horror of sin; the knowledge of his mysteries; confidence in his mercy; and a conviction, that we can never be saved but by his grace. He has announced these things, and then he finishes his career, by suffering for us, and pours forth his supplications to God. (Berthier)

Withhold not. The prophet now speaks in the name of Christ's mystical body, the Church, praying to be made a partaker of mercy, and to be delivered from evils, (Worthington) or Christ speaks as the victim for our sins. (Haydock) --- Uphold me. This might be also rendered as a prayer, "May thy," &c., with the Hebrew and some copies of the Septuagint. (Berthier)
